mainTopic: Vegetable vows in שביעית, vows on related foods, and singular versus plural wording in vows on wheat and beans
overview: The גמרא first limits the earlier משנה about someone who vows off 'vegetables' during שביעית. That person may still eat garden vegetables, but only where people do not bring vegetables in from חוץ לארץ. This ruling fits one side of a dispute between תנאים about whether such importing is allowed, and רבי ירמיה explains the stricter view: a clod of impure earth might come along. Then a new משנה teaches how far a vow on one food reaches to related foods: cabbage and ispargus, pounded beans and their stew, stew and its garlic, and lentils and אשישים. In each pair a vow on the basic item reaches the related item, but not the other way around. רבי יוסי is lenient in the dish cases. The משנה then deals with vows on wheat and pounded beans, and רבי יהודה allows chewing them raw. The גמרא brings a ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן גמליאל showing that the singular word, the plural word, or both together each forbid different forms of the food. The פרק of הנודר מן המבושל then closes with הדרן.

steps.title: The leniency applies only where vegetables are not imported
steps.stepSummary: The earlier משנה's ruling that a person who vows off 'vegetables' in שביעית may still eat garden vegetables applies only where people do not import vegetables from חוץ לארץ. Where they do import, he is forbidden in garden vegetables too.
steps.simpleTranslation: They only taught this in a place where people don't bring vegetables from outside ארץ ישראל into ארץ ישראל. But in a place where they do bring vegetables in from outside, he is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא puts a limit on the earlier משנה about vowing off vegetables during שביעית. The leniency for garden vegetables works only in a place where vegetables are not imported.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In שביעית, garden vegetables are normally not around, so the word 'vegetable' in his vow does not cover them. Where garden vegetables are brought in from חוץ לארץ, where the laws of שביעית do not apply, they are common again. So his vow includes them and he is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught [this ruling] in the case of…; a phrase that limits a ruling

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows a basic rule of נדרים: what a word in a vow covers depends on how people in that place and time actually use it.

phrases.english: They only taught [this] in a place
phrases.notes: This goes back to the משנה's ruling that someone who vows off 'vegetables' in שביעית may still eat garden vegetables.

phrases.english: where people do not bring vegetables
from outside the Land into the Land.
But in a place where they bring vegetables
from outside the Land into the Land, he is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the earlier משנה about vowing off vegetables in שביעית
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The leniency for garden vegetables in שביעית applies only where vegetables are not imported from חוץ לארץ. Where they are imported, he is forbidden.

steps.title: This matches a dispute between תנאים about importing vegetables
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says this distinction is like a dispute in a ברייתא. The first opinion says one may not bring vegetables from חוץ לארץ into ארץ ישראל. רבי חנניה בן גמליאל says one may.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like a dispute between תנאים. One opinion says we may not bring vegetables from outside the Land into the Land. רבי חנניה בן גמליאל says we may bring vegetables from outside the Land into the Land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא connects the rule it just taught to a dispute among תנאים about whether vegetables may be imported into ארץ ישראל at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the view that importing is forbidden, garden vegetables would not be available in שביעית, so the vow would never cover them. According to רבי חנניה בן גמליאל, importing is allowed, so there can be places where garden vegetables are common and the vow does cover them.

keyTerms.meaning: Like [a dispute of] תנאים; this question was already argued by earlier sages
They bring, or one may bring
A תנא who allows importing vegetables

phrases.english: Like [a dispute of] תנאים:
One may not bring vegetables
from outside the Land into the Land.
Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel says:
One may bring vegetables
from outside the Land into the Land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that step 1's distinction follows one side of a dispute between תנאים about importing vegetables
steps.raayaObject: The distinction between places that import vegetables and places that do not
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא with a dispute between תנאים about importing vegetables
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Step 1's distinction depends on a dispute between תנאים. The first opinion forbids bringing vegetables from חוץ לארץ into ארץ ישראל, and רבי חנניה בן גמליאל allows it. Only according to him can there be a place where imported garden vegetables are common.

steps.title: Why forbid importing vegetables?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind the opinion that vegetables may not be brought from חוץ לארץ into ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the one who says we may not bring them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a simple question about the stricter opinion: what is wrong with bringing vegetables in? It is setting up רבי ירמיה's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Importing vegetables seems harmless, so the stricter opinion needs a reason. The question is a real request for information, not an attack on either opinion.

phrases.english: What is the reason of the one who says
'one may not bring' [them]?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the first opinion in step 2
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason for forbidding the import of vegetables into ארץ ישראל

steps.title: רבי ירמיה: because of a clod of earth
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה explains that the worry is a clod of earth from חוץ לארץ that might come along with the vegetables.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said: because of a clod of earth.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה answers the question. The problem is not the vegetables themselves but the dirt that might come along with them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earth from חוץ לארץ carries טומאה. A clod stuck to the vegetables would bring that טומאה into ארץ ישראל, so the stricter opinion forbids importing.
steps.whatToRemember: Where vegetables are imported, garden vegetables are common even in שביעית, so a vow on 'vegetables' includes them. The view that forbids importing worries about a גוש of earth from חוץ לארץ.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said:
Because of a clod [of earth].
phrases.notes: He means dirt from outside the Land stuck to the vegetables. That earth is impure, and it would end up inside the Land.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The worry is that a clod of impure earth from חוץ לארץ would come in with the vegetables.

steps.title: משנה: cabbage and ispargus
steps.stepSummary: Someone who vows off cabbage is forbidden in ispargus. Someone who vows off ispargus may still eat cabbage.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If he vowed off cabbage, he is forbidden in ispargus. If he vowed off ispargus, he is permitted in cabbage.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It teaches that a vow on a general food includes its sub-type, but a vow on the sub-type does not include the general food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ispargus is a kind of cabbage, so 'cabbage' covers it. But 'ispargus' names only that specific kind, so regular cabbage stays permitted. The vow only works in one direction.
steps.confusionAlert: Ispargus here is a kind of cabbage, not the asparagus we know today.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
[If he vowed] from cabbage, he is forbidden in ispargus;
[if he vowed] from ispargus, he is permitted in cabbage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a new topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow on cabbage includes ispargus, but a vow on ispargus does not include cabbage.

steps.title: משנה: pounded beans and bean stew
steps.stepSummary: Someone who vows off pounded beans is forbidden in the stew made from them, but רבי יוסי permits it. Someone who vows off the stew may eat pounded beans.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he vowed off pounded beans, he is forbidden in the stew, and רבי יוסי permits it. If he vowed off the stew, he is permitted in pounded beans.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with pounded beans and a stew made from them. This is the first case in the משנה with a dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion holds that the beans are still there inside the stew, so a vow on beans covers the stew. רבי יוסי permits it, since the stew is a different dish from plain beans. In the other direction everyone agrees: a vow on the stew does not cover plain beans.

keyTerms.meaning: A thick stew, here made of pounded beans
The תנא who is lenient in this case and the next two

phrases.english: [If he vowed] from pounded beans, he is forbidden in the stew;
and Rabbi Yosei permits [it].
[If he vowed] from the stew, he is permitted in pounded beans.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִן הַגְּרִיסִין אָסוּר בְּמִקְפָּה וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי מַתִּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of food vows in the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the first opinion, a vow on pounded beans forbids the bean stew, while רבי יוסי permits it. A vow on the stew permits plain beans.

steps.title: משנה: stew and garlic
steps.stepSummary: Someone who vows off the stew is forbidden in its garlic, but רבי יוסי permits it. Someone who vows off garlic may eat the stew.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he vowed off the stew, he is forbidden in the garlic, and רבי יוסי permits it. If he vowed off garlic, he is permitted in the stew.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with stew and the garlic cooked in it. It follows the same pattern as the beans case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion treats the garlic in the stew as part of the stew, so a vow on the stew covers it. רבי יוסי again permits it. A vow on garlic does not forbid the stew.
steps.whatToRemember: A vow on a general item covers its sub-type or its parts, but not the other way around. רבי יוסי is lenient about foods that come from, or are cooked in, the item named in the vow.

phrases.english: [If he vowed] from the stew, he is forbidden in the garlic;
phrases.notes: This means the garlic that was cooked in the stew.

phrases.english: and Rabbi Yosei permits [it].
[If he vowed] from garlic, he is permitted in the stew.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִן הַמִּקְפָּה אָסוּר בִּשּׁוּם וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי מַתִּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same pattern as step 6
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the first opinion, a vow on the stew forbids its garlic, while רבי יוסי permits it. A vow on garlic permits the stew.

steps.title: Lentils and the lentil dish
steps.stepSummary: Someone who vows off lentils is forbidden in אשישים, a lentil dish, but רבי יוסי permits it. Someone who vows off אשישים may still eat lentils.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone vows off lentils, he may not eat אשישים (a dish made from lentils), but רבי יוסי allows it. If he vows off אשישים, he may eat plain lentils.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives one more food-and-dish pair in the same pattern as the last few cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נדר on the basic food reaches the dish made from it, because the dish is still mostly that food. רבי יוסי disagrees, as he did before. A נדר on the dish does not forbid the plain food, because the plain food is not that dish.

phrases.english: One who vows off lentils is forbidden in ashishim,
phrases.notes: אשישים is a dish made from lentils.

phrases.english: but Rabbi Yosei permits it.
One who vows off ashishim is permitted in lentils.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list of food-versus-dish cases from steps 5-7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A נדר on lentils forbids the lentil dish (רבי יוסי permits); a נדר on the dish does not forbid lentils.

steps.title: Vowing off wheat or pounded beans
steps.stepSummary: Someone who says 'wheat (singular), wheat (plural) that I taste' is forbidden in both flour and bread. Someone who says 'pounded bean, pounded beans that I taste' is forbidden in them both raw and cooked.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says, 'חטה, חטין, that I taste,' he is forbidden in wheat, whether as flour or as bread. If he says, 'גריס, גריסין, that I taste,' he is forbidden in pounded beans, whether raw or cooked.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה moves to a new kind of case. Here the question is not food versus dish, but how far a נדר on wheat or beans reaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person used both the singular and the plural word. Because of that, the נדר covers every form of the food: flour and bread for wheat, raw and cooked for beans. The ברייתא in steps 11-12 shows why using both words matters.
steps.confusionAlert: Notice that the person says BOTH the singular and the plural word. The ברייתא below shows that saying only one of them gives a narrower נדר.

phrases.english: 'Wheat, wheat grains, that I taste' —
phrases.notes: This is the language of a נדר: whatever wheat I taste is forbidden to me like a קרבן.

phrases.aramaic: אָסוּר בָּהֶן בֵּין קֶמַח בֵּין הַפַּת.
phrases.english: he is forbidden in them, whether flour or bread.
'Pounded bean, pounded beans, that I taste' —

phrases.aramaic: אָסוּר בָּהֶן בֵּין חַיִּין בֵּין מְבוּשָּׁלִין.
phrases.english: he is forbidden in them, whether raw or cooked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic in the משנה: the wording of a נדר on wheat and pounded beans.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Using both the singular and plural words forbids wheat as flour and bread, and beans both raw and cooked.

steps.title: רבי יהודה allows chewing raw
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says that if someone says 'קונם pounded bean or wheat that I taste,' he may still chew them raw.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: if someone says, 'Pounded bean or wheat is קונם, that I taste,' he is allowed to chew them raw.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה adds a limit to the נדר: chewing the raw grain or bean is not included.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People do not usually eat wheat or pounded beans by chewing them raw. So רבי יהודה holds that the person did not mean to include that when he made his נדר. Here he used the singular words, unlike the double wording in step 9.

keyTerms.meaning: A word used to make something forbidden like a קרבן

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
'Pounded bean or wheat is קונם, that I taste' —
he is permitted to chew them raw.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an exception to the wheat and bean rule of step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, a נדר on 'pounded bean or wheat' does not forbid chewing them raw.

steps.title: Singular and plural wording for wheat
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: 'חטה' forbids baked wheat but allows chewing; 'חטים' forbids chewing but allows baked; saying both forbids both.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: if he said 'חטה that I taste,' he is forbidden in baked wheat and allowed to chew grains. If he said 'חטים that I taste,' he is forbidden to chew grains and allowed baked wheat. If he said 'חטה, חטין, that I taste,' he is forbidden both to chew and to bake.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that explains why the משנה's double wording matters.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The singular word 'חטה' is taken to mean wheat as food, baked into bread. The plural 'חטים' is taken to mean the separate grains, which a person chews. Only saying both words covers both.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that in נדרים, a small change like singular versus plural can change exactly what becomes forbidden.

phrases.english: גמרא: It was taught in a ברייתא:
Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel says:
'Wheat (singular) that I taste' —
he is forbidden in baked wheat and permitted to chew.
'Wheat grains (plural) that I taste' —
he is forbidden to chew and permitted in baked wheat.
'Wheat, wheat grains, that I taste' —
he is forbidden both to chew and in baked wheat.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the double wording 'חטה חטין' in the משנה of step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Singular 'חטה' means baked wheat; plural 'חטים' means grains for chewing; saying both forbids both.

steps.title: Singular and plural wording for pounded beans
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: 'גריס' forbids cooked beans but allows chewing; 'גריסין' forbids chewing but allows cooked; saying both forbids both.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said 'גריס that I taste,' he is forbidden in cooked beans and allowed to chew them. If he said 'גריסין that I taste,' he is forbidden to chew them and allowed cooked. If he said 'גריס, גריסין, that I taste,' he is forbidden both cooked and chewed.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא repeats the same pattern, this time for pounded beans instead of wheat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The singular word means the cooked bean dish, which is how people usually eat it. The plural means the separate beans that one chews raw. Saying both words covers both, which explains the משנה's double wording for beans too.
steps.whatToRemember: In a נדר: the singular word points to the usual prepared food (bread or a cooked dish), the plural points to the raw grains or beans, and saying both forbids everything.

phrases.english: 'Pounded bean (singular) that I taste' —
he is forbidden in cooked beans and permitted to chew.
'Pounded beans (plural) that I taste' —
he is forbidden to chew and permitted in cooked beans.
'Pounded bean, pounded beans, that I taste' —
he is forbidden both in cooked beans and to chew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same singular and plural pattern from step 11 to pounded beans.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Singular 'גריס' means cooked beans; plural 'גריסין' means raw beans to chew; saying both forbids both.

steps.title: Hadran: Closing the chapter of הנודר מן המבושל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא ends the פרק with the traditional farewell line, 'We will return to you, הנודר מן המבושל.'
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, 'One who vows off cooked food.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is not a new argument. The גמרא is closing the פרק called הנודר מן המבושל with the traditional הדרן line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פרק is named after its first words, so this one is called הנודר מן המבושל. Saying הדרן עלך is a promise to come back and learn it again. The last topic before this line was the ברייתא of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל about חטה and חטים, and גריס and גריסין.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you. The traditional line said when finishing a פרק.
One who vows off cooked food. This is the name of the פרק, taken from its opening words.
A chapter of the משנה and גמרא.

steps.whatToRemember: The whole פרק of הנודר מן המבושל teaches one main idea. A נדר is understood the way people normally talk. So whether a word like 'cooked,' 'lentils,' or 'wheat' covers a food depends on everyday speech, and small changes in wording, like singular or plural, can change what is forbidden.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't look for a new הלכה in this line. הדרן עלך is only a closing formula and adds no new law.

phrases.english: We will return to you,
'One who vows off cooked food'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Formally closes the פרק after the final ברייתא about חטה and חטים, and גריס and גריסין.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פרק of הנודר מן המבושל is complete. Its main idea is that the meaning of a נדר follows ordinary everyday speech.
